deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of the closing article of Riemann's 1851 Göttingen dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. In the printed text this is the final section (Art. 20/22 depending on edition), which begins 'Die Einführung der complexen Grössen in die Mathematik hat ihren Ursprung und nächsten Zweck in der Theorie einfacher ... Abhängigkeitsgesetze zwischen veränderlichen Grössen'. The previous page ends the existence argument: z is a continuous function of the complex variable w in the surface T. The next page continues: 'den Weg vom Begriff zum Ausdruck ... allgemein zu ebnen war der Hauptzweck unserer bisherigen Untersuchungen'.

There are no computations on the page. It is a programmatic statement in three steps.

(1) Motivation. Complex quantities arose from the study of simple laws of dependence between variable quantities. Applied to complex arguments, these laws reveal an otherwise hidden harmony and regularity. Algebraic functions, circular functions, and elliptic and Abelian functions have successively shown that this extension both simplifies and enriches each theory.

(2) Programme. The principles developed so far (Cauchy–Riemann characterisation, Dirichlet-principle existence theorem, boundary and discontinuity conditions) determine a function completely, independently of any formula for it. From this general foundation one ascends to the various analytic expressions the function admits.

(3) Example: the characterisation of algebraic functions. Let the domain of z be spread one or more times over the whole infinite plane A, i.e. a compact branched covering of the Riemann sphere. Allow only isolated discontinuities, and only poles of finite order. A pole of order one means:
- at a finite point z', the function behaves like 1/(z−z');
- at z = ∞, it behaves like z itself.
Under these conditions the function is algebraic. In modern terms, a meromorphic function on a compact Riemann surface spread over P^1 satisfies a polynomial equation F(w, z) = 0. The converse holds in the printed text.

(4) Finite dimensionality. To obtain functions depending on only finitely many parameters, the boundary conditions must not prescribe arbitrary data at every point along a line. There are two ways to achieve this:
- (a) Extend T over the whole plane, so that no boundary remains (a closed surface).
- (b) The general case: between 2 or 2n parts of the boundary, relations between the values of w are fixed. The surface can then be enlarged beyond one boundary piece, without changing the function, while being correspondingly shrunk along the paired piece. The piece cut off at one side has a counterpart at the other that is similar in its smallest parts, i.e. conformally equivalent.

In modern terms, (b) is pairing boundary arcs by conformal identifications: a fundamental domain with side pairings, as with periods or periodicity moduli. The result is effectively a closed Riemann surface, so the space of admissible functions with prescribed singularities is finite-dimensional.

I (the analyst) add the following clarification. The finiteness claim rests on the earlier existence and uniqueness theorem: a function on a closed surface is determined by its singular parts up to finitely many constants, a precursor of Riemann's inequality / Riemann–Roch.
errors: No mathematical errors. The statements are qualitative and unproved here; the proofs are by reference to the earlier articles.

The claim that the conditions yield an algebraic function is asserted without argument on this page. Rigorous proof needs the existence theory (Dirichlet principle), which was later criticised by Weierstrass. The assertion itself is correct.
The description of boundary pairing in step (4b) is vague. It works as a heuristic for fundamental domains with conformal side identifications, but is not a precise construction.

results.what: Programmatic principle: a complex function is defined by intrinsic conditions (domain, singularities, boundary behaviour), independently of any analytic expression, and its expressions are then derived.
results.modern_name: Riemann's conceptual (geometric) approach to function theory

results.what: A function on a finitely-sheeted surface covering the whole extended plane, with only finite-order poles as singularities, is algebraic. Order is measured by 1/(z−z') at finite points and by z at infinity.
results.modern_name: Meromorphic functions on compact Riemann surfaces are algebraic (Riemann existence theorem / characterization of algebraic functions)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (dissertation, final article); fully in 1857 Abelian functions paper

results.what: Finitely many parameters are obtained by removing the boundary entirely (closed surface), or by pairing 2 or 2n boundary parts via conformal relations so the surface is effectively closed.
results.modern_name: Gluing a fundamental domain by side pairings to form a closed Riemann surface; finite-dimensionality of function spaces with prescribed singularities
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 dissertation (final article); later Klein, Poincaré for fundamental domains

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the well-known concluding article of Riemann's 1851 dissertation; the wording closely matches the printed text. The only interest is minor draft variants, e.g. 'Ausgangspunkt' vs the printed 'Ursprung', and the deleted/inserted words.

checkable.asserts: 1/(z−z') has a simple pole at z = z' with residue 1, i.e. it is an infinitely large quantity of first order.
z itself is of first order at z = ∞: in the local coordinate t = 1/z it behaves like 1/t.
1/(z−z') is complex-differentiable away from z', consistent with the Art. 1 definition of a function of a complex variable.

Toy example of boundary pairing: identifying the two boundary lines of a horizontal strip of width 2π via w -> w + 2πi leaves exp(w) unchanged, i.e. one side can be extended while the paired side is shrunk.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'den Ausgangspunkt und nächsten Zweck' is correct per the image. The printed version has 'Ursprung und nächsten Zweck'.
Line 1–2: 'der Theorie der ver-/änderlichen[?] Größen' should probably read 'der Theorie der imaginären Größen' or similar. The image shows 'der Theorie der ei.../glegen Größen'; uncertain.
Line 3: 'zwischen [?] veränderlichen Größen' is likely 'zwischen zwei veränderlichen Größen'; uncertain.
The deleted word at the end of the first paragraph ('[-bereichert-]') appears struck through, with possibly 'erweitert' in the printed text; the reading is uncertain.
'unter den früher aufgelegten Grenzbedingungen' is probably 'früher aufgestellten Grenzbedingungen'.
'in einfache[?] gleiche[?] Relationen' is likely 'einfache gegenseitige Relationen' or 'einfache gleichförmige Relationen'; illegible in part.
